fast.topic:
The Monday fast hour: the whole of GST_112 Week 1 in a single pass. The only available material is the MIVA recap deck.

It opens with culture, defined as a complex system of traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values. Then it drills the three fundamental components - technological (material culture), sociological (institutions and norms), and ideological (beliefs and values). That list is the week's most examinable.

Next it moves to society, categorised into communal and associational forms. The two are distinguished on three fixed bases: division of labour, social interactions, and traditions.

Then the historical emergence of society, through two lenses. Karl Marx's vision of a communist society built on collective ownership of the means of production and distribution of wealth. And functionalism's view of society as an organism in which each component plays a crucial role.

Then the impact of colonialism on African societies - specifically its alteration of governance, culture and family structures. Pre-colonial Yoruba communities are the worked example.

The hour closes on nation-building, defined as mobilising resources for socio-economic and political development while constructing a national identity. Then national integration: why it matters for a diverse country, Nigeria's ethnic-diversity hurdle, and government initiatives to foster unity.

Reference facts are drilled at the end. Cosmas Odinaka's 2020 study on nation-building and national integration. And the University of Lagos Centre for General Studies text Nigerian Peoples and Cultures (Lagos, 2013).

deep.topic:
This session takes Week 1 conceptually.

What problem-solving in computer science is, and why a computer demands a systematic approach. The computer contributes volume, speed and efficiency, not method. So the programmer must first know how a human solves the problem.

What makes a problem a computational problem: a step-by-step solution with well-defined inputs, limitations and output conditions.

The four steps to problem-solving, treated as four distinct jobs rather than a list to recite.

What each of algorithm, pseudocode and flowchart actually is, and what each buys you. Including why pseudocode that cannot be compiled or executed is still worth writing.

The three required properties of an algorithm's steps (ordered, unambiguous, complete), and what specifically breaks when each is absent.

Decomposition: why it works, and where it stops working.

Then the translator chain of interpreter, compiler and assembler, the difference between debugging and testing, and the three error types of syntax, logical and run time.

fast.topic:
The Wednesday fast hour covers GST_122 Week 1, "Language Skills". It establishes listening, speaking, reading and writing as the four building blocks of effective communication.

It fixes the course's exact definition of each skill. Listening is understanding, interpreting and responding to spoken language. Speaking is articulating thoughts, ideas and information coherently and effectively. Reading is comprehending, interpreting and analysing written text. Writing is conveying thoughts, information and emotions through written language.

It draws the distinction between hearing and listening. Then between active listening (full engagement, as in a lecture) and passive listening (merely hearing without deep comprehension, as with background music).

On speaking, it covers the components of oral communication - clear pronunciation, appropriate tone, audience engagement, voice control, body language and delivery. These are worked through a persuasive-speech structure and two contrasting job-interview answers.

On reading, it covers reading comprehension as grasping main ideas, context and subtext. The passage is "The Dangers of Faking Mental Health Issues", with its four takeaways.

On writing, it names the four writing styles: persuasive, descriptive, narrative and expository.

The hour closes with the marketing-team case study on emotive language and precision. Then the claim that combining the skills strengthens critical thinking, engagement with complex discourse and a global perspective.

Focus effort on stating definitions verbatim, and on classifying given examples to the right skill or style. That is how the course examines.

fast.topic:
The Thursday fast hour covers PHY_108 Week 1: the review of the equation of a straight line, and error analysis. Both underpin every practical report this semester.

It starts with y = mx + c. Identify the dependent and independent variable. Read the gradient from two points on a best-fit line. Then the y-intercept c, and the x-intercept as -c/m.

It then drills linearisation. T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) converts into T^2 against L, with slope 4*pi^2/g. N = N0*e^(-lambda*t) converts into ln N against t, with slope -lambda and intercept ln N0. y = kx^n converts into log y against log x, with slope n and intercept log k. Plus the Hooke's law, Coulomb's law and Boyle's law rows of the same table.

Next it covers the graphing rules that carry marks in a lab report - sensible scaling, labelled axes with units, accurate plotting, and a single best-fit line rather than dot-to-dot.

The error half defines error as the difference between measured and true value. It separates systematic from random error, with their sources. It gives absolute error, relative or fractional error, percentage error, and the signed percentage difference.

It closes with the Week 1 case study idea that the mean of repeated measurements is the most likely value. Then the Ohm's law framing from the week summary, where V is plotted against I so the gradient gives the resistance.

Work one numerical example end to end: gradient to g to percentage error.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x + 3. For which input x is the output f(x) = 11?
questions.concept: Finding the input for a given output
questions.why:
Set 2x + 3 = 11, so 2x = 8 and x = 4. Check: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11.

x = 25 is f(11), evaluating instead of solving; x = 7 comes from adding 3 instead of subtracting it (2x = 14); x = −4 is a sign slip when the 3 is moved across (2x = −8).

questions.q: f(x) = x² + 1 has domain {0, 1, 2, 3}. An arrow diagram sends each input into the codomain {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 12}. What is the range of f?
questions.concept: Range versus codomain in an arrow diagram
questions.why:
The range is the set of outputs actually produced: f(0) = 1, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 5, f(3) = 10, so R = {1, 2, 5, 10}.

{0, 1, 2, 3} is the domain; {7, 12} are the codomain values that no arrow reaches; the full six-element set is the codomain, which is what was offered, not what was hit.

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 4. Evaluate f(−3).
questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic at a negative input
questions.why:
Square first, then subtract: (−3)² − 4 = 9 − 4 = 5.

−13 treats (−3)² as −9; 49 subtracts before squaring, (−3 − 4)²; −10 uses 2x in place of x², giving 2(−3) − 4.

questions.q: Find the domain of f(x) = (2x − 3)/(x² + 9).
questions.concept: Domain when the denominator never vanishes
questions.why:
The denominator must not be zero: x² + 9 ≠ 0 means x² ≠ −9, and no real number squares to a negative, so nothing is excluded and D = (−∞, ∞).

ℝ \ {−9} solves x + 9 = 0 instead of x² + 9 = 0; ℝ \ {3/2} excludes the zero of the numerator, which never restricts a domain; ℝ \ {−3, 3} treats x² = −9 as if it were x² = 9.

questions.q: Find the range of f(x) = 3 − |x + 1|.
questions.concept: Range of an absolute value function
questions.why:
|x + 1| ≥ 0. Multiplying by −1 reverses the inequality: −|x + 1| ≤ 0. Adding 3 does not: 3 − |x + 1| ≤ 3, so y ≤ 3 and R = (−∞, 3]. The value 3 is attained at x = −1.

[3, ∞) forgets that multiplying by −1 flips the sign; (−∞, −1] reads the −1 inside the absolute value as if it were an output bound; [−3, ∞) keeps the wrong direction and also loses the sign of the 3.

questions.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 5.
questions.concept: Inverse of a linear function
questions.why:
Let y = 2x + 5, switch to x = 2y + 5, isolate y: 2y = x − 5, so y = (x − 5)/2. Check: f(1) = 7 and f⁻¹(7) = (7 − 5)/2 = 1.

(x + 5)/2 loses the sign when the 5 is moved across; 1/(2x + 5) is the reciprocal, not the inverse; 2x − 5 undoes the addition but forgets to divide by 2.

questions.q: A straight-line graph passes through the points (0, 2), (1, 3) and (2, 4). Which rule does it represent?
questions.concept: Reading a rule from points on a graph
questions.why:
Each point is (x, f(x)). Test the rule at all three: 0 + 2 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 2 = 4, so f(x) = x + 2.

f(x) = 2 − x gives 2, 1, 0, a line falling instead of rising; f(x) = 2x gives 0, 2, 4 and fits only the last point; f(x) = x + 1 gives 1, 2, 3, the right slope but the wrong intercept.

questions.q: A rule sends A → K, B → 3, C → 9 and D → 3, where K is a letter, not a number. Which description is correct?
options: Not a function, because 3 is hit twice
Not a function, because K is not a number
questions.concept: Real-valued versus function
questions.why:
Each input has exactly one output, so the rule is a function. 'Real-valued' adds a condition on the outputs: they must be real numbers. K is not, so the function is not real-valued.

A repeated output (3 twice) never disqualifies a function; only an input with two arrows would. K breaks the real-valued condition, not the function condition.

questions.q: f(x) = 3x + 1 and g(x) = x². Find (f ∘ g)(x) and the value of (f ∘ g)(2).
questions.concept: Forming a composite function
questions.why:
f ∘ g means f[g(x)]: drop x² into the x-slot of f, so f[x²] = 3(x²) + 1 = 3x² + 1. Then (f ∘ g)(2) = 3(2)² + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13, which you can also get as g(2) = 4 then f(4) = 13.

9x² + 6x + 1 is g ∘ f, the composition done in the wrong order. 3x³ + x² multiplies the two functions instead of substituting one into the other, and x² + 3x + 1 adds them.

questions.q: Find the range of f(x) = 4x − 7 by making x the subject.
questions.concept: Range of a linear function by making x the subject
questions.why:
Let y = 4x − 7. Then 4x = y + 7 and x = (y + 7)/4. That formula returns a real x for every real y, with no division by zero and no root of a negative, so every y is an output and the range is (−∞, ∞), all of ℝ.

[−7, ∞) and (−∞, −7] mistake the constant term for a bound, and [7/4, ∞) treats the root x = 7/4 of f as if it limited the outputs.

questions.q: f(x) = 3 − x. List the points (x, f(x)) for x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and say whether y rises or falls as x increases.
questions.concept: Tabulating a function for plotting
questions.why:
Substitute each input: f(0) = 3, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1, f(3) = 0, so the points are (0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 0). The coefficient of x is −1, so y drops by 1 for every 1 that x gains: y falls.

The values 3, 4, 5, 6 come from x + 3 instead of 3 − x, and −3, −2, −1, 0 come from x − 3. Keeping the right values but saying y rises reads the sign of the gradient backwards.

questions.q: One relation sends the input 4 to both 2 and −2. A second relation sends 2 to 4 and −2 to 4. Which of these is a function?
options: Only the second, because an input may not have two outputs but an output may be repeated
Only the first, because an output may not come from two different inputs
Both, because every pair listed is allowed
Neither, because each one repeats a number
questions.concept: Definition of a function applied to a relation
questions.why:
A function assigns exactly one output to each input. The first relation gives the single input 4 two outputs, 2 and −2, so it breaks that condition and is not a function. The second gives 2 → 4 and −2 → 4: each input still has exactly one output, and nothing forbids two inputs sharing an output, which is exactly what f(x) = x² does.

The other options invert the rule (restricting outputs instead of inputs) or treat a repeated output as a fault.

questions.q: An object carries a net charge of −6.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ C. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many excess electrons does it hold?
questions.concept: Counting electrons with q = ne
questions.why:
q = ne, so n = |q|/e = 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.0 × 10² = 400 electrons. The charge is negative, so they are excess electrons.

2.5 × 10⁻³ divides the wrong way round (e/q); 1.0 × 10⁻³⁵ multiplies q by e instead of dividing; 4.0 × 10³ is a power-of-ten slip when subtracting the exponents (−17 − (−19) = 2, not 3).

questions.q: Rubbing an ebonite rod with fur moves 5.0 × 10¹¹ electrons from the fur to the rod. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What are the charges on the rod and on the fur afterwards?
questions.concept: Charge transferred by friction from an electron count
questions.why:
q = ne = (5.0 × 10¹¹)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ C. The rod gained electrons, so it is −8.0 × 10⁻⁸ C; the fur lost the same electrons, so it is +8.0 × 10⁻⁸ C. Check: the total is still zero, as before rubbing.

The first option has the signs backwards (the receiver of electrons is negative); −3.1 × 10³⁰ C divides n by e instead of multiplying; 'fur 0' forgets that charge is conserved, so the fur must carry the equal and opposite charge.

questions.q: Two identical metal spheres carry −8.0 nC and +2.0 nC. They are touched together and then separated. What charge does each sphere carry afterwards?
questions.concept: Charge sharing between identical conductors
questions.why:
Charge is conserved and identical spheres share it equally: q′ = (q₁ + q₂)/2 = (−8.0 + 2.0)/2 = −6.0/2 = −3.0 nC on each.

−5.0 nC ignores the sign of the +2.0 nC and averages 8 and 2; −6.0 nC is the total, not halved; +3.0 nC drops the sign of the larger charge.

questions.q: Point charges of +2.0 μC and +3.0 μC are held 3.0 cm apart in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the force between them?
questions.concept: Coulomb's law with two charges
questions.why:
Convert 3.0 cm to 0.030 m and square it: r² = 9.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². F = kq₁q₂/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(9.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 5.4 × 10⁻²/9.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 60 N. Both charges are positive, so the force is repulsive.

1.8 N forgets to square r (divides by 0.030); 6.0 × 10⁻³ N leaves r in centimetres (divides by 9); 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ N reads μC as 10⁻⁹ C and gets the direction wrong as well.

questions.q: Two fixed point charges repel with a force F. The separation between them is then halved, with the charges unchanged. What is the new force?
questions.concept: Inverse-square dependence of the Coulomb force
questions.why:
F ∝ 1/r². Replacing r by r/2 gives 1/(r/2)² = 4/r², so the force becomes 4F.

2F treats the law as 1/r; F/4 has the dependence upside down (a smaller gap must give a larger force); F/2 combines both errors.

questions.q: A point charge Q = +4.0 nC is fixed in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Find the electric field at a point 2.0 cm from Q.
questions.concept: Field of a point charge
questions.why:
E = kQ/r² with r = 0.020 m, r² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²: E = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 36/4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 9.0 × 10⁴ N/C. The field of a positive charge points away from it.

9.0 N/C leaves r in centimetres (divides by 4); 1.8 × 10³ N/C forgets to square r; the 'toward Q' option has the magnitude right but the direction of a positive charge's field wrong.

questions.q: At a point P the electric field is 5.0 × 10³ N/C pointing north. A charge of −2.0 μC is placed at P. What force acts on it?
questions.concept: Force on a charge in a field, F = qE
questions.why:
F = |q|E = (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(5.0 × 10³) = 1.0 × 10⁻² N. The field direction is defined for a positive charge, so a negative charge feels the force the opposite way: south.

The 'north' option forgets the sign reversal; 2.5 × 10⁹ N divides E by q instead of multiplying; 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ N reads μC as 10⁻⁹ C.

questions.q: A positively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand. The sphere is earthed for a moment, the earth wire is removed, then the rod is taken away. What is the sphere's final charge?
options: Positive on the near side, negative on the far side
questions.concept: Sign of the charge left by induction
questions.why:
The positive rod pulls the sphere's free electrons to the near side and leaves the far side positive. Earthing lets electrons flow up from the earth to cancel that positive far side, so the sphere now has extra electrons. Removing the earth wire first traps them; when the rod goes, they spread out. The sphere is negative, opposite to the rod.

'Zero' is what happens if the rod is removed before the earth wire; 'positive' is the sign given by conduction (touching), not induction; the separated near/far pattern is polarisation while the rod is present, not the final state.

questions.q: A test charge of +2.0 nC placed at a point P feels a force of 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ N directed west. What is the electric field at P, and what does it become if the test charge is replaced by +6.0 nC?
questions.concept: Field from the force on a test charge, E = F/q₀
questions.why:
E = F/q₀ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ / 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ = 3.0 × 10⁴ N/C, and the test charge is positive, so E points the way the force does: west. Replacing it with +6.0 nC triples the force to 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ N, but E = F/q₀ is still 3.0 × 10⁴ N/C, because the field belongs to the source charges and not to whatever is placed in it.

East reverses the direction for a positive test charge; 9.0 × 10⁴ N/C makes the field follow the force; 3.3 × 10⁻⁵ N/C divides q₀ by F instead of F by q₀.

questions.q: Point charges of +3.0 μC and −3.0 μC attract each other with a force of 8.1 N in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the separation between them?
questions.concept: Finding the separation from Coulomb's law
questions.why:
Rearrange F = kq₁q₂/r² to r² = kq₁q₂/F = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)/8.1 = 8.1 × 10⁻²/8.1 = 1.0 × 10⁻² m², so r = 0.10 m, or 10 cm.

0.010 m is r² reported as r, the square root step forgotten; 10 m comes from inverting the fraction to r² = F/kq₁q₂; 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m reads the charges as nanocoulombs.

questions.q: At a point 5.0 cm from an isolated point charge Q the electric field is 7.2 × 10⁴ N/C, pointing toward Q. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is Q?
questions.concept: Finding a source charge from its field
questions.why:
E = k|Q|/r², so |Q| = Er²/k = (7.2 × 10⁴)(0.050)²/(9.0 × 10⁹) = (7.2 × 10⁴)(2.5 × 10⁻³)/(9.0 × 10⁹) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C. The field points toward Q, and field lines run into negative charges, so Q = −2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C, or −20 nC.

−4.0 × 10⁻⁷ C forgets to square r; −2.0 × 10⁻⁴ C leaves r in centimetres; +2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C has the right size but the wrong sign.

questions.q: A negatively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand. The sphere is never earthed. Which describes the sphere while the rod is near, and after the rod is taken away?
options: Near side negative, far side positive; net charge zero throughout
Near side positive, far side negative; the sphere is left positive after the rod goes
The sphere gains a net negative charge while the rod is near, and keeps it
Near side positive, far side negative; net charge zero throughout, and unpolarised after the rod goes
questions.concept: Polarisation of a conductor without earthing
questions.why:
The rod is negative, so it repels the sphere's free electrons to the far side and leaves the near side positive. Nothing enters or leaves the sphere, because there is no path to earth, so the net charge stays zero at every stage; once the rod is removed the electrons spread back and the sphere is neutral and unpolarised again.

The first option moves the electrons toward the rod instead of away; the second and third describe induction with earthing, which this sphere never had.

questions.concept: Tracing a flowchart decision
questions.why:
A = 4 and B = 9, so the test A > B is 4 > 9, which is false. The No branch runs: B − A = 9 − 4 = 5 is printed.

−5 takes the Yes branch and prints A − B; 13 adds the two inputs instead of subtracting; 9 prints the larger input rather than the difference.

questions.q: A student does four things while solving a problem. P: writes the pseudocode and draws the flowchart. Q: lists the inputs, the processing and the output. R: rewrites the working program to run faster with the same results. S: types the program in and runs it. Which order follows the four steps to problem-solving?
questions.concept: Ordering the four problem-solving steps
questions.why:
The four steps are: understand the problem (Q, inputs, processes, output), create a step-by-step plan (P, algorithm as pseudocode and flowchart), carry out the plan (S, code and run it), then evaluate and refactor (R). So Q, P, S, R.

P, Q, S, R plans before understanding the problem; Q, S, P, R codes before any plan exists; Q, P, R, S refactors a program that has not yet been written.

questions.q: A translator takes a program written in Java and produces assembly language, which still has to be translated once more before the CPU can run it. Which translator is this?
questions.concept: Identifying the translator from its input and output
questions.why:
High-level language in, assembly language out is the compiler. The assembly still needs an assembler to become machine code, which is why one more translation remains.

An interpreter takes high-level language too, but goes straight to machine code with no second stage; an assembler takes assembly language as its input, not Java; the CPU runs machine code and translates nothing.

questions.q: A grade program is accepted by the compiler with no complaints, runs to the end without stopping, and prints an average of 36 for five grades that actually average 45. Which type of error is this?
options: Not an error, since the program ran
questions.concept: Classifying an error as syntax, logical or run time
questions.why:
The program was built and ran to completion, yet the answer is wrong. An error that leaves the program running happily while producing the wrong result is a logical error.

A syntax error would have stopped the compiler accepting the program; a run time error would have stopped the run part way through; a wrong answer is an error whether or not the program finished.

questions.q: A plan reads: 1. Read the five grades. 2. Add them and divide by 5. 3. If the result is high enough, print PASS; otherwise print FAIL. 4. Stop. Which required property of an algorithm's steps does the plan break?
questions.concept: Identifying which algorithm property a step violates
questions.why:
Step 3 says "high enough" without saying what that means, so two programmers would write two different tests. The steps are not unambiguous.

The steps are in a workable order (read, compute, decide, stop), so ordered holds; both outcomes PASS and FAIL are handled, so complete holds; "none" ignores the vague condition in step 3.

questions.q:
How many grades does this pseudocode read?

```
count = 1
total = 0
WHILE count < 5
    READ g
    total = total + g
    count = count + 1
ENDWHILE
```
questions.concept: Counting loop iterations
questions.why:
count starts at 1 and the body runs while count < 5, so it runs for count = 1, 2, 3, 4. Four grades are read. When count becomes 5 the test fails and the loop ends.

5 assumes the test is count ≤ 5 or that count starts at 0; 6 counts up to and including the failing test; 3 stops one iteration early by treating count = 4 as the exit.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 4
    IF i is even THEN
        total = total + i
    ELSE
        total = total - i
    ENDIF
ENDFOR
PRINT total
```
questions.concept: Tracing a loop with a decision inside
questions.why:
i = 1 is odd: total = 0 − 1 = −1. i = 2 is even: −1 + 2 = 1. i = 3 is odd: 1 − 3 = −2. i = 4 is even: −2 + 4 = 2. So 2 is printed.

10 adds every i and ignores the ELSE branch; −2 swaps the two branches (add odd, subtract even); 4 is only the last i, forgetting that total accumulates.

questions.q: A grade program works correctly. Which of these changes to it is NOT a refactor?
options: Replacing five separate additions with a loop that gives the same total
Changing the pass mark in the decision from 45 to 50
Renaming G1 to grade1 everywhere it appears
Deleting a variable that is never read
questions.concept: Refactoring preserves function
questions.why:
Refactoring improves the structure, design or efficiency of a working solution without changing what it does. Changing the pass mark changes which students pass, so the function changes: that is a change of specification, not a refactor.

The loop, the rename and the deleted dead variable all leave every output exactly as it was, so each of those is a refactor.

questions.q: Which pseudocode prints HOT when T is above 30, WARM when T is from 20 to 30 inclusive, and COLD otherwise?
options: IF T > 20 THEN PRINT WARM; ELSE IF T > 30 THEN PRINT HOT; ELSE PRINT COLD
IF T > 30 THEN PRINT HOT; ELSE IF T >= 20 THEN PRINT WARM; ELSE PRINT COLD
IF T > 30 THEN PRINT HOT; ELSE IF T > 20 THEN PRINT WARM; ELSE PRINT COLD
IF T >= 30 THEN PRINT HOT; ELSE IF T >= 20 THEN PRINT WARM; ELSE PRINT COLD
questions.concept: Writing pseudocode with a three-way decision
questions.why:
The tests run in order, so T > 30 takes everything above 30 to HOT, and whatever is left meets T >= 20, which catches 20 up to 30 inclusive; the rest is COLD. Check the boundaries: T = 20 gives WARM, T = 30 gives WARM, T = 31 gives HOT.

Using T > 20 for the second test sends T = 20 to COLD. Using T >= 30 for the first test sends T = 30 to HOT instead of WARM. Testing T > 20 first sends T = 35 to WARM, because the HOT test below it is never reached.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
total = 1
FOR i = 1 TO 4
    total = total * 2 + i
ENDFOR
PRINT total
```
questions.concept: Tracing an accumulator step by step
questions.why:
total starts at 1. i = 1: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3. i = 2: 3 × 2 + 2 = 8. i = 3: 8 × 2 + 3 = 19. i = 4: 19 × 2 + 4 = 42. So 42 is printed.

68 adds i before doubling, (total + i) × 2; 19 stops one pass early at i = 3; 16 doubles four times and never adds i.

questions.q:
This is meant to read N numbers and print their average, but for N = 3 it never finishes.

```
READ N
count = 0
total = 0
WHILE count < N
    READ x
    total = total + x
ENDWHILE
PRINT total / N
```

Which repair is correct, and what does the repaired program print for N = 3 with inputs 4, 7, 10?
options: Add `count = count + 1` inside the loop body; it prints 7
Add `count = count + 1` after ENDWHILE; it prints 7
Add `count = count + 1` inside the loop body; it prints 21
Add `N = N + 1` inside the loop body; it prints 7
questions.concept: Spotting the missing loop update
questions.why:
count never changes inside the loop, so count < N stays true forever. Putting count = count + 1 in the body lets count reach 3 and stop the loop; total is 4 + 7 + 10 = 21 and 21 / 3 = 7 is printed.

An update placed after ENDWHILE leaves the loop untouched, so it still never ends; 21 forgets the division by N; raising N inside the loop pushes the target further away every pass, so the loop still never ends.

questions.q: Three faulty steps appear in a plan that averages five grades and prints PASS or FAIL. (i) "Compute the average of the five grades" is placed before "Read the five grades". (ii) "If the average is good enough, print PASS". (iii) There is a PASS step but no FAIL step. Which required property of an algorithm's steps does each one break, taken in the order (i), (ii), (iii)?
questions.concept: Ordered, unambiguous and complete steps
questions.why:
(i) computes with values that have not been read yet, so the steps are out of order. (ii) says "good enough" without a number, so two programmers would write two different tests: it is ambiguous. (iii) leaves a grade below the mark with no output at all, so a case is missing and the plan is not complete.

Every other ordering pairs the vague condition or the missing FAIL branch with the wrong property; only ordered, unambiguous, complete matches each fault to what it actually breaks.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 1.

Evaluate f(x) = 2x + 3 and f(x) = x² − 4 at negative inputs.

Find domains by setting the denominator ≠ 0, including the case her rendered examples never reach, where the exclusion is real.

Find ranges by making x the subject, and by building up from |·| ≥ 0.

Find inverses by let–switch–isolate.

Form and expand both composites of f(x) = 5x − 4 and g(x) = x².

Then work her TASK: the domain and range of √(x + 2) − 8, plus the corrected table from slide 22.

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 4. Find and simplify f(a + 1).
questions.concept: Evaluating a function at an algebraic expression
questions.why:
Replace every x by (a + 1): (a + 1)² − 4 = a² + 2a + 1 − 4 = a² + 2a − 3.

a² − 3 squares term by term and drops the 2a cross term; a² + 2a + 1 expands the square but forgets the −4; a² + 2a + 5 adds 4 instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: Find the domain of f(x) = (x + 1)/(x² − 5x + 6).
questions.concept: Domain of a rational function by factoring the denominator
questions.why:
Set the denominator ≠ 0: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), which is zero at x = 2 and x = 3, so D = ℝ \ {2, 3}.

ℝ \ {−2, −3} has the signs of the roots backwards; ℝ \ {−1, 2, 3} also excludes the zero of the numerator, which never restricts a domain; ℝ \ {6} excludes the constant term instead of solving the quadratic.

questions.q: Find the range of f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) by making x the subject.
questions.concept: Range of a rational function by making x the subject
questions.why:
y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) gives y(x − 3) = 2x + 1, so xy − 2x = 3y + 1 and x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2). This is a real number for every y except y = 2, so R = ℝ \ {2}.

(−∞, ∞) forgets the division by y − 2; ℝ \ {3} is the domain, not the range; ℝ \ {−1/2} is the x-intercept mistaken for a missing output.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x − 3 and g(x) = x² + 1. Evaluate (g ∘ f)(3).
questions.concept: Evaluating a composite at a number
questions.why:
g ∘ f means f runs first: f(3) = 2(3) − 3 = 3, then g(3) = 3² + 1 = 10.

17 is (f ∘ g)(3), the wrong order (g(3) = 10, then f(10) = 17); 30 multiplies f(3) and g(3); 13 adds them.

questions.q: f(x) = 3x − 2 and g(x) = x². Find (g ∘ f)(x) in expanded form.
questions.concept: Expanding a squared composite
questions.why:
g ∘ f = g[f(x)] = (3x − 2)² = (3x − 2)(3x − 2) = 9x² − 6x − 6x + 4 = 9x² − 12x + 4.

9x² + 4 squares each term separately and loses both cross terms; 3x² − 2 is f ∘ g, the other order; 9x² − 6x + 4 keeps only one of the two −6x terms.

questions.q: f(x) = 3x − 7. Find f⁻¹(5).
questions.concept: Evaluating an inverse at a number
questions.why:
f⁻¹(5) is the input that f sends to 5: 3x − 7 = 5, so 3x = 12 and x = 4. Equivalently f⁻¹(x) = (x + 7)/3 and (5 + 7)/3 = 4.

8 is f(5), evaluating instead of inverting; −2/3 is (5 − 7)/3, a sign slip in the inverse; 1/8 is the reciprocal 1/f(5), not the inverse.

questions.q: Find the domain of f(x) = √(4 − 2x).
questions.concept: Domain of a square root with a negative coefficient
questions.why:
The quantity under the root cannot be negative: 4 − 2x ≥ 0, so −2x ≥ −4, and dividing by −2 reverses the inequality: x ≤ 2. D = (−∞, 2].

[2, ∞) forgets to reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative; (−∞, −2] drops the sign of the 4 when moving it across (−2x ≥ 4); [−2, ∞) makes both of those errors at once.

questions.q: For f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3), a student cancels to x + 3 and states the domain as ℝ. What is the correct domain of f?
questions.concept: Domain is fixed before cancelling
questions.why:
The domain is decided by the function as given, before any cancelling: the denominator x − 3 is zero at x = 3, so f(3) is undefined and D = ℝ \ {3}. Cancelling produces x + 3, which agrees with f everywhere except at that one missing point.

ℝ ignores the division by zero; ℝ \ {−3} excludes a zero of the numerator instead; ℝ \ {−3, 3} excludes both roots of the numerator, which never restrict a domain.

questions.q: Find the domain and the range of h(x) = √(x + 6) − 4.
questions.concept: Domain and range of a square root function
questions.why:
The quantity under the root cannot be negative, so x + 6 ≥ 0 and x ≥ −6, giving D = [−6, ∞). Since √(x + 6) ≥ 0, subtracting 4 gives h(x) ≥ −4, so R = [−4, ∞); nothing was multiplied by a negative, so no inequality reverses.

Both brackets are square because x = −6 is a legal input and h(−6) = −4 is actually reached. [6, ∞) has the sign of the boundary wrong, [0, ∞) forgets the −4, and the round brackets wrongly exclude endpoints that are attained.

questions.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 2)/4.
questions.concept: Finding and verifying an inverse
questions.why:
Let y = (3x − 2)/4, switch the letters to get x = (3y − 2)/4, then isolate y: 4x = 3y − 2, 3y = 4x + 2, y = (4x + 2)/3. Checking, f(f⁻¹(x)) = (3·(4x + 2)/3 − 2)/4 = 4x/4 = x, so f⁻¹(x) = (4x + 2)/3 is right.

(4x − 2)/3 loses the sign when the −2 is moved across, 4/(3x − 2) is the reciprocal rather than the inverse, and (3x + 2)/4 never switches x and y at all.

questions.q: Find the domain of f(x) = √(x − 1)/(x − 4).
questions.concept: Domain with a root and a denominator
questions.why:
Two restrictions apply at once. The root needs x − 1 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 1, and the denominator needs x − 4 ≠ 0, so x ≠ 4. Putting them together gives [1, 4) ∪ (4, ∞), also writeable as x ≥ 1 with x ≠ 4.

[1, ∞) forgets the denominator, ℝ \ {4} forgets the root, and (1, 4) ∪ (4, ∞) wrongly throws out x = 1, where f(1) = 0/(−3) is perfectly defined.

questions.q: The range of h(x) = 2 − |x − 3| is (−∞, 2]. Why is the bracket at 2 square while the bracket at −∞ is round?
options: A square bracket always marks a maximum and a round bracket always marks a minimum
y = 2 is attained, at x = 3, while −∞ is not a number and is never attained
h is defined at x = 2 but is undefined at x = −∞
y = 2 is never quite reached, while the values run all the way down to −∞
questions.concept: Square versus round brackets in interval notation
questions.why:
A square bracket says the endpoint is actually attained, a round bracket says it is not. At x = 3 the absolute value is 0, so h(3) = 2 and the output 2 really is reached, which earns the square bracket. On the other side −∞ is not a number at all: h just keeps falling without ever landing on it, so that end stays round.

The maximum-versus-minimum option invents a rule that does not exist, and the option about h being defined at x = 2 confuses an input with an output.

checks.topic:
This session takes the same week-1 material and works it as problems.

Converting between a net charge and a number of transferred electrons using q = ne.

Tracking charge through transfers, including the averaging rule q' = (q1+q2)/2 for identical conducting spheres in contact, and following a charge through two successive contacts.

Computing Coulomb forces, with attention to squaring the separation and converting centimetres to metres.

Adding forces and fields as vectors. That includes the case of two equal and opposite charges whose contributions at the midpoint reinforce rather than cancel, and finding the point on a line where the resultant field vanishes.

Computing the field of a point charge and the force it exerts on a charge placed in it, including the direction reversal for a negative charge.

Also diagnosing a wrong route from the shape of a formula, and checking a result by units and by order of magnitude.

Constants used throughout: k = 8.99x10^9 N.m^2.C^-2, e = 1.6x10^-19 C.

questions.q: Sphere X carries −16 nC. It is touched to an identical neutral sphere Y and separated. Y is then touched to an identical neutral sphere Z and separated. What charge does Z carry?
questions.concept: Charge through two successive contacts
questions.why:
Each contact between identical spheres halves the charge in play. First contact: X and Y each get (−16 + 0)/2 = −8.0 nC. Second contact: Y and Z each get (−8.0 + 0)/2 = −4.0 nC. So Z has −4.0 nC (and X keeps −8.0 nC).

−8.0 nC stops after the first contact; −5.3 nC splits −16 nC three ways as if all three spheres touched at once; −2.0 nC halves one time too many.

questions.q: Charges are fixed on the x-axis: +2.0 μC at x = 0, +1.0 μC at x = 0.20 m and −1.0 μC at x = 0.30 m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the net force on the +1.0 μC charge?
questions.concept: Net force from two collinear charges
questions.why:
From the +2.0 μC charge (0.20 m away): F₁ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.20)² = 0.018/0.040 = 0.45 N, repulsive, so in the +x direction. From the −1.0 μC charge (0.10 m away): F₂ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.10)² = 0.0090/0.010 = 0.90 N, attractive, toward x = 0.30 m, so also +x. Both point the same way: net = 0.45 + 0.90 = 1.35 N in the +x direction.

0.45 N subtracts the two forces as if they opposed; 0.90 N ignores the +2.0 μC charge; the −x option has the direction of the attraction backwards.

questions.q: Point charges of +4.0 μC and −2.0 μC are fixed 0.20 m apart. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the resultant electric field at the midpoint between them?
questions.concept: Superposition of fields at the midpoint
questions.why:
Each charge is 0.10 m from the midpoint. E from +4.0 μC = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.10)² = 3.6 × 10⁶ N/C, pointing away from it, that is toward the −2.0 μC charge. E from −2.0 μC = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.10)² = 1.8 × 10⁶ N/C, pointing toward the −2.0 μC charge. Same direction, so they add: 5.4 × 10⁶ N/C toward the −2.0 μC charge.

1.8 × 10⁶ N/C subtracts the two fields as if they opposed; the 'toward +4.0 μC' option has the direction reversed; 1.35 × 10⁶ N/C uses the full 0.20 m separation instead of the 0.10 m to the midpoint.

questions.q: In a hydrogen atom the electron is 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m from the proton. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the electric force between them?
questions.concept: Coulomb force between electron and proton
questions.why:
Both charges have magnitude e. F = ke²/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/(5.3 × 10⁻¹¹)² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.56 × 10⁻³⁸)/(2.81 × 10⁻²¹) = 2.30 × 10⁻²⁸/2.81 × 10⁻²¹ = 8.2 × 10⁻⁸ N. Opposite signs, so attractive.

The 'repulsive' option gets the sign of the interaction wrong; 4.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ N forgets to square r; 5.1 × 10¹¹ N uses e once instead of e².

questions.q: A +1.0 μC charge sits at the origin. A +3.0 μC charge is at x = 0.10 m and a −4.0 μC charge is at y = 0.10 m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the magnitude of the net force on the +1.0 μC charge?
questions.concept: Adding perpendicular Coulomb forces
questions.why:
From +3.0 μC: F = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.10)² = 2.7 N, repulsive, pushing the charge along −x. From −4.0 μC: F = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁶)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.10)² = 3.6 N, attractive, pulling along +y. The two are perpendicular, so the resultant is √(2.7² + 3.6²) = √(7.29 + 12.96) = √20.25 = 4.5 N.

20.25 N forgets the square root; 6.3 N adds the magnitudes as if they were parallel; 0.90 N subtracts them as if they were opposite.

questions.q: Sphere A carries −6.0 nC and sphere B carries +2.0 nC. The spheres are not the same size. They are touched together and separated, and A is found to carry −1.0 nC. What charge does B now carry?
questions.concept: Conservation of charge in a transfer
questions.why:
Charge is conserved: the total before is −6.0 + 2.0 = −4.0 nC, and the total after must also be −4.0 nC. B has whatever A does not: −4.0 − (−1.0) = −3.0 nC.

−2.0 nC assumes the spheres are identical and share equally, which the stem rules out; +3.0 nC has the sign of the remainder wrong; −4.0 nC gives B the whole total and forgets that A still carries −1.0 nC.

questions.q: At a distance d from a point charge Q the electric field has magnitude E₀. What is the field at a distance 3d from a charge 3Q?
questions.concept: Scaling E with both charge and distance
questions.why:
E = kQ/r². Tripling Q multiplies E by 3; tripling r divides it by 3² = 9. Together: 3/9 = 1/3, so the field is E₀/3.

E₀ treats the distance dependence as 1/r, so the two factors of 3 cancel; 3E₀ changes the charge but forgets the distance; E₀/9 forgets the charge.

questions.q: The field at a point is found by measuring the force on a +1.0 nC test charge and dividing by 1.0 nC. The test charge is replaced by +3.0 nC and the measurement is repeated. How do the force and the field compare with before?
questions.concept: Field as a property of the source, not the test charge
questions.why:
F = qE. The field at the point is set by the source charges alone, so E is the same; the force on a three-times-larger test charge is three times larger. Dividing the tripled force by the tripled charge returns the same E.

'Field tripled' confuses E with F; 'force unchanged' forgets that F scales with q; 'field one third' divides the same force by a larger charge, but the force is not the same.

questions.q: An electron is placed 2.0 cm from a fixed point charge of +5.0 nC in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the field at the electron's position, and the force on the electron?
options: 1.1 × 10⁵ N/C; 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N directed away from the charge
2.3 × 10³ N/C; 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ N directed toward the charge
1.1 × 10⁵ N/C; 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N directed toward the charge
11 N/C; 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁸ N directed toward the charge
questions.concept: Field of a point charge then force on an electron
questions.why:
E = kQ/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(5.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.020)² = 45/4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.125 × 10⁵ N/C, pointing away from the positive charge. Then F = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(1.125 × 10⁵) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, and the electron is negative, so the force is opposite to E: toward the +5.0 nC charge.

'Away' forgets the electron's sign; 2.3 × 10³ N/C leaves r unsquared; 11 N/C keeps r in centimetres.

questions.q: A +1.0 μC charge is fixed at x = 0 and a +9.0 μC charge at x = 0.40 m. At which point between them is the resultant electric field zero?
questions.concept: Locating the point where two fields cancel
questions.why:
Between two positive charges the two fields oppose, so they cancel where the magnitudes match: k(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/x² = k(9.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.40 − x)². Cancel k and take square roots: (0.40 − x)/x = √9 = 3, so 0.40 = 4x and x = 0.10 m, that is 0.10 m from the smaller charge.

x = 0.040 m uses the ratio 9 without taking its root; x = 0.30 m puts the null nearer the larger charge; x = 0.20 m is the midpoint, which would only work for equal charges.

questions.q: Identical conducting spheres carrying +10 nC and −2.0 nC are touched together, separated, and placed with their centres 4.0 cm apart. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the force between them?
questions.concept: Charge sharing followed by Coulomb's law
questions.why:
Identical spheres share the total charge equally, so each ends with q′ = (+10 − 2.0)/2 = +4.0 nC. Then F = kq′²/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹)²/(0.040)² = 1.44 × 10⁻⁷/1.6 × 10⁻³ = 9.0 × 10⁻⁵ N, and both spheres are now positive, so it is repulsive.

1.1 × 10⁻⁴ N attractive uses the original charges and skips the contact; 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ N averages +10 and +2.0, dropping the minus sign; 3.6 × 10⁻⁶ N forgets to square r.

questions.q: Two identical metal spheres, one carrying +6.0 nC and one neutral, are touched together and separated. A student says both now carry +6.0 nC, since the charge spreads onto the second sphere. What is wrong, and what are the true charges?
options: It breaks quantisation of charge; each sphere carries +3.0 nC
Nothing is wrong; each sphere carries +6.0 nC
It breaks conservation of charge; each sphere carries +3.0 nC
It breaks conservation of charge; the first keeps +6.0 nC and the second stays neutral
questions.concept: Conservation of charge applied to a contact
questions.why:
The student's answer makes the total +12 nC where it was +6.0 nC, so charge would have been created. Conservation of charge forbids that: the charge is shared, not copied, and identical spheres split it equally, giving (+6.0 + 0)/2 = +3.0 nC each with the total still +6.0 nC.

Quantisation is about charge coming in multiples of e and is not broken here; +6.0 nC each is the student's own error; leaving the second sphere neutral ignores that contact between conductors does share charge.

checks.topic:
This session is Week 1 applied - the method worked through on concrete problems.

You trace the lecture's student-grade flowchart on real numbers: five grades, average, pass mark 45, decision box "Is Grade > 44". That includes the boundary case where the average lands exactly on 45. He then alters the decision box to "Is Grade > 45" and works out precisely which candidates are misclassified as a result.

He reads a faulty pseudocode that sums four grades but divides by five. He identifies the fault, classifies it against the three error types, and reasons about which test inputs would and would not expose it.

He runs step 1 of the four steps on the inventory management case study, separating genuine inputs, processes and outputs from outcomes and from the tools themselves. He then decomposes that case study into subproblems, and distinguishes real decomposition from mere phasing, delegation or file-splitting.

He classifies stated scenarios into the four computational problem types, particularly the optimization-versus-search and decision-versus-search boundaries.

Finally he diagnoses a failed attempt by another student, and locates which of the four steps actually went wrong.

Reading, tracing and applying rather than reciting.

questions.q:
Trace this pseudocode with the inputs 50, 42, 46, 38, 49. Give the value of Grade and what is printed.

```
READ G1, G2, G3, G4, G5
Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4 + G5) / 5
IF Grade > 44 THEN
    PRINT "PASS"
ELSE
    PRINT "FAIL"
ENDIF
```
questions.concept: Tracing the grade-average pseudocode
questions.why:
Sum: 50 + 42 + 46 + 38 + 49 = 225. Grade = 225 / 5 = 45. The test 45 > 44 is true, so PASS is printed.

Grade = 45 with FAIL misreads the test as Grade > 45; Grade = 44 drops G5 and divides the remaining 176 by 4; 35.2 drops G5 but still divides by 5.

questions.q: A program prints PASS when Grade > 44 and FAIL otherwise. Someone changes the test to Grade > 45. Four students have averages 44, 44.8, 45 and 46. Which of them are printed PASS by the original program but FAIL by the changed one?
questions.concept: Effect of changing a decision condition on boundary inputs
questions.why:
Original test Grade > 44: 44 FAIL, 44.8 PASS, 45 PASS, 46 PASS. Changed test Grade > 45: 44 FAIL, 44.8 FAIL, 45 FAIL, 46 PASS. The results differ for 44.8 and 45.

"45 only" forgets that a non-whole average between 44 and 45 is caught too; "44 and 44.8" treats the original test as Grade ≥ 44; "44, 44.8 and 45" thinks 44 passed the original test, but 44 > 44 is false.

questions.q: Five grades between 0 and 100 are read one at a time in a loop whose body is `READ g` followed by one IF line; after the loop, `PRINT low`. Which starting value and IF line together print the lowest grade?
options: `low = 100` and `IF g < low THEN low = g`
`low = 0` and `IF g < low THEN low = g`
`low = 100` and `IF g > low THEN low = g`
`low = 100` and `IF g < low THEN g = low`
questions.concept: Choosing the correct implementation of a minimum search
questions.why:
Start low above every possible grade, then replace it whenever a smaller grade appears: low = 100 with IF g < low THEN low = g. After five grades low holds the smallest one. For 70, 35, 90, 35, 60 it ends at 35.

Starting at 0 means no grade is ever below low, so 0 is printed; testing g > low with a start of 100 never updates and prints 100; low = g written backwards as g = low changes the grade, not low, so 100 is printed.

questions.q:
Complete the missing line so the program prints how many of the five grades are 45 or more.

```
passed = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 5
    READ g
    IF g >= 45 THEN
        ______
    ENDIF
ENDFOR
PRINT passed
```
questions.concept: Completing a counter inside a loop
questions.why:
Each grade of 45 or more must add one to the count, so the line is passed = passed + 1. For grades 45, 30, 60, 44, 45 it prints 3.

passed = passed + g adds the grades themselves, printing 150 for that input; passed = 1 can never rise above 1 however many pass; passed = i stores the position of the last passing grade, 5, rather than a count.

questions.q:
This should print 45.0 for these grades but prints 9.6. Which change fixes it?

```python
grades = [52, 38, 47, 40, 48]
for g in grades:
    total = 0
    total = total + g
print(total / 5)
```
options: Change `total = total + g` to `total = total + grades`
questions.concept: Locating a misplaced initialisation from wrong output
questions.why:
total = 0 sits inside the loop, so every iteration throws away the running total and total ends as the last grade alone: 48 / 5 = 9.6. Moving total = 0 above the for line makes the sum 225 and prints 45.0.

len(grades) is 5 already, so that change prints 9.6 again; adding the whole list to a number is a type error and the program stops; printing inside the loop prints five numbers, the last still 9.6.

questions.q: A program is to be written to decide which products a shop should reorder. Which of these is an input to that program?
options: The list of products to reorder
Last month's sales count for each product
The spreadsheet package used to run it
questions.concept: Separating inputs, processes and outputs
questions.why:
Inputs are the data the program is given to work on. Last month's sales per product is exactly that: it exists before the program runs and the reorder decision is computed from it.

The reorder list is the output the program produces; fewer lost sales is an outcome the shop hopes for after using the output, not data at all; the spreadsheet package is a tool the program runs in, not something it takes in.

questions.q: "Of all the possible order quantities for a product, which one gives the lowest total cost while staying within the budget?" Which type of computational problem is this?
questions.concept: Classifying computational problem types
questions.why:
The answer is not just any quantity that fits the budget but the best one, the lowest cost. When the best possible solution is the only accepted solution, the problem is an optimization problem.

A search problem would accept any quantity with the property (within budget); a counting problem would ask how many quantities fit; a decision problem would ask a YES or NO question such as "is there a quantity within budget?".

questions.q: A student writing the reorder program never wrote down what "low stock" should mean. Her program compiles, runs and passes every test she wrote, but it reorders products the shop is not short of. Which of the four problem-solving steps went wrong?
questions.concept: Diagnosing which problem-solving step failed
questions.why:
The program does exactly what she planned and coded; the trouble is that the plan was built on an undefined idea of "low stock". The inputs, limits and output conditions were never pinned down, which is the job of the first step, understanding the problem.

The plan and the code faithfully carried out her misunderstanding, so steps 2 and 3 did their jobs; refactoring cannot fix a program that solves the wrong problem.

questions.q: Five grades are read into G1, G2, G3, G4 and G5. Which pair of lines sets Grade to the average of all five and prints PASS exactly when that average is 45 or more?
options: `Grade = G1 + G2 + G3 + G4 + G5 / 5` then `IF Grade >= 45 THEN PRINT PASS ELSE PRINT FAIL`
`Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4) / 5` then `IF Grade >= 45 THEN PRINT PASS ELSE PRINT FAIL`
`Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4 + G5) / 5` then `IF Grade >= 45 THEN PRINT PASS ELSE PRINT FAIL`
`Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4 + G5) / 5` then `IF Grade > 45 THEN PRINT PASS ELSE PRINT FAIL`
questions.concept: Correct pseudocode for a grade average and decision
questions.why:
All five grades must be added inside brackets before the division, and the pass test must include the boundary, so it is Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4 + G5) / 5 with IF Grade >= 45. For 50, 42, 46, 38, 49 that gives 225 / 5 = 45 and prints PASS.

Without the brackets only G5 is divided by 5, giving 185.8 for the same grades; dropping G5 from the sum divides 176 by 5 and gives 35.2; Grade > 45 fails a student whose average is exactly 45.

questions.q:
This pseudocode has a fault: the sum leaves out G5 while the divisor stays 5.

```
READ G1, G2, G3, G4, G5
Grade = (G1 + G2 + G3 + G4) / 5
IF Grade > 44 THEN PRINT "PASS" ELSE PRINT "FAIL"
```

On which set of five grades do the faulty version and the corrected version print different words?
questions.concept: Choosing test inputs that expose a fault
questions.why:
The faulty Grade is short by G5 / 5. For 50, 50, 50, 50, 50 it is 200 / 5 = 40, which prints FAIL, while the corrected value 250 / 5 = 50 prints PASS, so the words differ.

For 60, 60, 60, 60, 0 both give 48 and print PASS, because G5 is 0 and the fault costs nothing. For 30, 30, 30, 30, 30 the values 24 and 30 are both at or below 44, so both print FAIL. For 80, 80, 80, 80, 10 the values 64 and 66 are both above 44, so both print PASS.

questions.q:
Trace this with N = 4 and the pairs (stock, point) = (3, 5), (12, 5), (5, 5), (7, 10). What does it print, in order?

```
READ N
low = 0
FOR i = 1 TO N
    READ stock, point
    IF stock <= point THEN
        PRINT "Reorder", i
        low = low + 1
    ENDIF
ENDFOR
PRINT low
```
questions.concept: Tracing a loop with a decision and a boundary case
questions.why:
i = 1: 3 ≤ 5 is true, so Reorder 1 and low = 1. i = 2: 12 ≤ 5 is false, nothing printed. i = 3: 5 ≤ 5 is true because the test is ≤ and not <, so Reorder 3 and low = 2. i = 4: 7 ≤ 10 is true, so Reorder 4 and low = 3. The last line prints 3.

Dropping product 3 reads the test as stock < point; Reorder 2 with Reorder 3 comes from reversing it to stock >= point; printing all four ignores the decision entirely.

questions.q: A shop's reorder problem is to be broken down before any code is written. Which of these proposals is a genuine decomposition of the problem?
options: Handle the fast-selling products this month and the slow-selling ones next month
Read the stock and sales figures; work out each product's reorder point; compare stock with that point; print the order list
Write the whole program first, then cut the finished code into three files
Give the stock counting to one member of staff and the ordering to another
questions.concept: Decomposition versus phasing and file-splitting
questions.why:
Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller problems, each solvable on its own, whose solutions combine into the whole. Reading the figures, computing reorder points, comparing, and printing are four such subproblems.

Splitting the work across two months is phasing in time: each month still faces the whole undivided problem. Cutting finished code into files divides the product rather than the problem, and happens after the thinking is done. Handing parts to two people is delegation, which shares the work without making any part simpler.

checks.topic: Culture's three components, the two society types, functionalism, colonialism's impact and nation-building.

questions.q: A people's hoes, looms, cooking pots and the houses they build are being studied. Which component of culture do these belong to?
questions.concept: Three components of culture
questions.why: Tools, artefacts and built objects are material culture, which is the technological component. Sociological would be the institutions and norms that govern people; ideological would be their beliefs and values. Associational is a type of society, not a component of culture.

questions.q: Communal and associational societies differ on three bases. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.concept: Communal vs associational society
questions.why: The three bases are division of labour, social interactions and traditions. Religion is a plausible outsider: it is part of culture, but it is not one of the three bases used to separate the two types of society.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that a village's family, market and shrine each do a job that keeps the whole community alive, like the organs of a body. Which perspective is this?
questions.concept: Functionalism
questions.why: Functionalism views society as an organism in which each component plays a crucial role, exactly the organ-of-a-body picture. Marx frames society around collective ownership of the means of production and wealth distribution, not organs and roles. Nation-building is a process of development and identity construction, and colonialism is foreign rule, so neither is a theory of how society works.

questions.q: Under foreign rule a pre-colonial Yoruba community had its chiefs replaced, its customs reshaped and its households reorganised. Which three domains of African society does this show colonialism altering?
questions.concept: Impact of colonialism on African societies
questions.why: Colonialism altered governance (the chiefs), culture (the customs) and family structures (the households). The other options name real colonial changes in places, but they are not the three domains identified for African societies, and each swaps in at least one domain that is not on the list.

questions.q: Which of the following is the definition of culture?
options: Collective ownership of the means of production and distribution of wealth
Mobilising resources for development and constructing a national identity
A complex system of traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values
A grouping of people into communal or associational forms
questions.concept: Definition of culture
questions.why: Culture is a complex system encompassing traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values. Collective ownership of the means of production is Karl Marx's communist society; mobilising resources and constructing a national identity is nation-building; grouping people into communal or associational forms describes society, not culture.

checks.topic: Internet vs Web, the request cycle, server types, and the tools you build with.

questions.q: A student opens `https://portal.miva.edu.ng:8443/courses/csc106/index.html?week=1`. What is the host part of this URL?
questions.concept: Parts of a URL: scheme, host, path
questions.why:
A URL reads scheme://host:port/path?query. Here the scheme is https, the host is portal.miva.edu.ng, the port is 8443, the path is /courses/csc106/index.html and the query is week=1.

https is the scheme, the protocol used to fetch the resource; /courses/csc106/index.html is the path to the resource on that host; miva.edu.ng drops the portal label, which is part of the host name the browser actually looks up.

questions.q: In `http://www.example.com/blog/2026/post.html#top`, which part is the path?
questions.concept: Parts of a URL: path versus fragment
questions.why:
The path begins at the first slash after the host and ends before any ? or #: /blog/2026/post.html. The #top fragment is handled by the browser, which scrolls to the element with id top; it is not sent to the server.

www.example.com/blog mixes the host with the start of the path; #top is the fragment; blog/2026/post.html#top drops the leading slash and keeps the fragment, which is not part of the path.

questions.q: A user clicks a link. Which is the correct order of the four steps that follow?
options: Browser renders the page → browser sends HTTP request → server sends HTTP response → server processes it
Browser sends HTTP request → server processes it → server sends HTTP response → browser renders the page
Server sends HTTP request → browser processes it → browser sends HTTP response → server renders the page
Browser sends HTTP response → server processes it → server sends HTTP request → browser renders the page
questions.concept: Order of the client-server request cycle
questions.why:
The client always initiates: the browser sends an HTTP request to the web server, the server processes it and retrieves the resource, the server sends an HTTP response back, and the browser renders and displays the content.

Rendering cannot come first because nothing has arrived yet; the server never sends the request, it answers one; the browser sends a request and receives a response, never the other way round.

questions.q: A dashboard greets you by the name stored in the database, and a menu drops down when you tap it. Which side does each job?
options: Browser fetches the name; server opens the menu
Server fetches the name; browser opens the menu
questions.concept: Splitting a task between client and server
questions.why:
Reading a record from the database is server work: the server stores and manages data and generates dynamic content from it. Opening a menu is a change to what the user sees, so it is the browser's job (front-end, user interface).

The browser cannot read the database directly; the server never draws anything on the screen; neither side does both, because the client-server model separates the two concerns.

questions.q: A request for /orders reaches a machine that runs the checkout code, checks the session and works out the total, then asks a second machine for rows from the orders table. Name the two server types, in order.
questions.concept: Identifying server types from their jobs
questions.why:
Running application-specific code, managing sessions and computing results is what an application server does (Node.js is the usual example). Storing structured data in tables and answering queries for rows is a database server (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB).

Database then application reverses the order of the two calls; a web server only serves stored files and routes HTTP requests, and a proxy server sits between clients and servers for caching, load balancing and filtering, so neither runs checkout logic or holds tables.

questions.q: You need to (a) get back yesterday's working copy of index.html and (b) find out why one image request took three seconds to load. Which tool category handles each?
options: (a) Browser developer tools, (b) Version control system
(a) Version control system, (b) Browser developer tools
questions.concept: Matching a job to a web development tool category
questions.why:
A version control system such as Git keeps a version history, so a past copy of a file can be rolled back to. Browser developer tools analyse network traffic and show how long each request took.

Developer tools do not store old versions of your files; a text editor and an IDE edit and debug code but neither keeps a history of yesterday's copy nor times network requests.

questions.q: One machine receives every incoming request, forwards each one to one of six backend servers, and keeps copies of popular images so the backends are not asked for them again. What type of server is it?
questions.concept: Recognising a proxy server
questions.why:
Distributing requests across backends is load balancing and keeping copies of popular content is caching; both are jobs of a proxy server, which sits between clients and other servers.

An application server runs the application code itself rather than forwarding requests; a database server stores structured data, not cached images; a web browser is the client that sends requests, not a machine that receives them.

questions.q: Four tasks on a shop site: (1) write the SQL that saves an order, (2) animate the cart icon when an item is added, (3) hash the password before storing it, (4) lay out the checkout page in HTML. Which are back-end?
questions.concept: Sorting tasks into front-end and back-end
questions.why:
Back-end work runs on the server and touches databases and server-side logic: saving an order with SQL (1) and hashing a password before storage (3). Animating an icon (2) and laying out a page in HTML (4) are what the user sees, so they are front-end.

2 and 4 are the front-end pair; 1 and 4 mixes a database task with page layout; 1, 3 and 4 wrongly counts HTML layout as server work.

questions.q: Each developer keeps a full copy of the repository on their own laptop and merges feature branches into a shared copy on a website. Which tool provides the local copies and branching, and what hosts the shared copy?
questions.concept: Git versus GitHub
questions.why:
Git is the version control system: it is distributed, so every developer holds a full copy, and it is known for branching and merging. GitHub (or GitLab) is a hosting platform that keeps the shared repository online and adds collaboration features.

GitHub; Git swaps the software for the hosting site; Visual Studio Code is a text editor, not version control; Nginx is a web server, which serves pages rather than hosting repositories.

questions.q: Which of these four is web server software?
questions.concept: Recognising web server software
questions.why:
Apache, together with Nginx and Microsoft IIS, is web server software: it stores web content and answers HTTP requests from browsers.

Eclipse is an IDE; PostgreSQL is a database server; Firefox is a web browser, the client that sends the requests a web server answers.

questions.q: What is the World Wide Web?
options: An application of interconnected pages joined by hyperlinks, running on the Internet
The global network of interconnected computers and devices
The protocol browsers use to fetch pages from servers
The address that specifies where a web resource is located
questions.concept: Internet versus World Wide Web
questions.why:
The World Wide Web is an application built on top of the Internet: web pages linked to one another by hyperlinks, introduced by Sir Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.

The global network of devices is the Internet itself, the infrastructure the Web runs on; the protocol for fetching pages is HTTP; the address of a resource is a URL.

questions.q: In the client-server model, what is the client?
options: The machine that stores web content and answers requests for it
The set of rules that carries a request across the network
The address bar entry that names the resource
The program, such as a browser or mobile app, that initiates a request for a resource
questions.concept: Definition of the client in the client-server model
questions.why:
The client is whatever initiates communication by requesting a service or resource: typically a web browser or a mobile app. The server is the other party, which processes the request and delivers the content.

The machine that stores and answers is the server; the rules that carry the request are the protocol, HTTP; the address bar entry is a URL, not a party in the model.

checks.topic: The four language skills, their definitions, active versus passive listening, speaking components and writing styles.

questions.q: Bola sits through a two-hour seminar, follows every argument and can restate the main points afterwards. Dayo has the radio on while cooking and cannot say what was discussed. Classify Bola and Dayo in that order.
questions.concept: Active versus passive listening
questions.why:
Active listening is full engagement, as during a lecture; passive listening is merely hearing without deep comprehension, as with background music. Bola is fully engaged, Dayo is not.

Swapping the two labels reverses the definitions; reading comprehension concerns written text, and oral communication is a speaking skill, not a listening one.

questions.q: Kemi studies a novel and works out how its symbolism shapes the story, paying attention to the main ideas, the context and the subtext. Which skill is she exercising?
questions.concept: Classifying a scenario to a language skill
questions.why:
Effective reading involves understanding main ideas, context and subtext, and analysing a novel's symbolism is the model case of reading comprehension.

Active listening deals with spoken input, expository writing is a writing style for explaining a topic, and oral communication is the delivery side of speaking.

questions.q: A newspaper column titled 'Why You Must Exercise Daily' opens by stating the writer's position and then piles up reasons to make the reader agree. Which writing style is this?
questions.concept: Identifying a writing style
questions.why:
The four writing styles are persuasive, descriptive, narrative and expository. A text that takes a side and works to convince the reader is persuasive.

Descriptive writing paints a detailed picture, narrative tells events in sequence, and expository explains a topic neutrally without arguing a side.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four key takeaways of the comprehension passage 'The Dangers of Faking Mental Health Issues'?
questions.concept: Key takeaways of the mental health comprehension passage
questions.why:
The four takeaways are Undermining Legitimacy, Obstructing Access to Support, Misallocation of Resources, and Honesty and Understanding. Hospital funding is never mentioned in the passage.

The other three options are all genuine takeaways, so picking one of them means the list was not learned.

questions.q: Which language skill is defined as the ability to articulate thoughts, ideas and information coherently and effectively?
questions.concept: Definition of speaking
questions.why:
Speaking is the ability to articulate thoughts, ideas and information coherently and effectively.

Writing is the capacity to convey thoughts, information and emotions through written language; listening is to understand, interpret and respond to spoken language; reading is to comprehend, interpret and analyse written text.

checks.topic: The straight-line equation, linearising the pendulum, error types, percentage difference and the best-fit rule.

questions.q: Water is heated and its temperature θ is plotted against time t. The best-fit line passes through (2.0 min, 37.0 °C) and (6.0 min, 45.0 °C). Find the gradient and the y-intercept.
questions.concept: Gradient and intercept from two points on a best-fit line
questions.why:
Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (45.0 − 37.0)/(6.0 − 2.0) = 8.0/4.0 = 2.0 °C/min. Then c = y − mx at either point: 37.0 − 2.0(2.0) = 33 °C, the temperature at t = 0.

8.0 °C/min takes the rise in θ without dividing by the time interval; 2.0 °C/min with 37 °C reads the first point's y-value as the intercept instead of going back to t = 0; 0.5 °C/min is Δx/Δy, the reciprocal of the gradient.

questions.q:
Simple pendulum readings:
L (m): 0.40, 0.65, 0.90
T (s): 1.27, 1.62, 1.90
The best-fit line of T² against L passes through the first and last points. Take π² = 9.87. Find g.
questions.concept: Finding g from a T² against L graph
questions.why:
Square the periods first: T² = 1.61 s² and 3.61 s². Gradient = (3.61 − 1.61)/(0.90 − 0.40) = 2.00/0.50 = 3.99 s² m⁻¹. Since T² = (4π²/g)L, the gradient equals 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/gradient = 39.48/3.99 = 9.88 m s⁻².

3.99 m s⁻² stops at the gradient and calls it g; 31.3 m s⁻² uses T instead of T² on the y-axis (gradient 1.26); 158 m s⁻² multiplies the gradient by 4π² instead of dividing.

questions.q: Five measurements of a line: 12.3, 12.5, 12.4, 14.6, 12.2 cm. Discard the one reading that is clearly an outlier, take the mean of the rest, and find its percentage difference from the reference length 12.6 cm.
questions.concept: Percentage difference of a mean after discarding an outlier
questions.why:
14.6 cm sits 2 cm from the others, which agree within 0.3 cm, so it is discarded. Mean of the remaining four = (12.3 + 12.5 + 12.4 + 12.2)/4 = 12.35 cm. Percentage difference = (observed − reference)/reference × 100 = (12.35 − 12.6)/12.6 × 100 = −2.0 %. The sign is negative because the observed value is below the reference.

+1.6 % keeps the outlier in the mean (12.8 cm); −0.25 % quotes the absolute difference in cm as if it were a percentage; +2.0 % drops the sign, which percentage difference must keep.

questions.q: A count follows N = N₀e^(−λt). The best-fit line of ln N against t passes through (0 s, 6.91) and (20 s, 4.91). Take e^6.91 ≈ 1000. Find λ and N₀.
questions.concept: Decay constant and N₀ from a ln N against t graph
questions.why:
Taking ln of both sides: ln N = −λt + ln N₀, a straight line with gradient −λ and intercept ln N₀. Gradient = (4.91 − 6.91)/(20 − 0) = −0.10 s⁻¹, so λ = 0.10 s⁻¹. The intercept is ln N₀ = 6.91, so N₀ = e^6.91 ≈ 1000.

λ = −0.10 s⁻¹ forgets that the gradient is −λ, not λ; N₀ = 6.91 reads the intercept as N₀ without undoing the logarithm; λ = 10 s⁻¹ is Δt/Δ(ln N), the reciprocal of the gradient.

questions.q: In timing 20 oscillations of a pendulum, a student always starts the stopwatch about 0.2 s after the bob is released, on every one of five trials. What type of error is this, and will averaging the five trials remove it?
options: Systematic error; averaging does not remove it
Random error; averaging does not remove it
questions.concept: Systematic versus random error
questions.why:
The delay has the same size and the same direction every trial, so every reading is short by about 0.2 s. A consistent one-way bias is a systematic error, and averaging readings that all share the same bias leaves the bias in the mean.

Random error would scatter both ways from trial to trial (a late start on one, an early start on the next) and would shrink with averaging; that is not what is described. Systematic error can only be removed by correcting for it, for example by subtracting the known delay or timing from a mid-swing reference point.

recapCandidates.topic: Charging by induction versus charging by conduction: why contact leaves the same sign and no contact leaves the opposite one.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Both methods start with a charged rod near a conductor, so the two get filed as one procedure, and the earthing step is remembered as a place where charge is 'drained off' rather than as the step that selects which sign stays behind.
whyQuestions: Which particles actually move when any object is charged, and which never do?
In conduction, why do the rod and the sphere end up with the same sign?
In induction the rod never touches the sphere, so where does the sphere's charge come from?
Why must the earth connection be broken before the rod is taken away, and not after?
The rod loses charge in conduction but not in induction. Why does that difference follow from the mechanisms rather than being an extra fact to memorise?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It says that only electrons move, in both methods, and that the sign of an object is decided by whether it has gained or lost them.
It explains conduction as direct sharing on contact - charge flows until the two bodies are at the same potential, so both carry the same sign and the rod is left with less than it began with.
It explains induction as separation followed by selective removal: the rod's field pushes like charge to the far side, earthing lets exactly that charge escape, and breaking the earth first traps the imbalance, leaving the opposite sign while the rod's own charge is untouched because nothing crossed the gap.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A negatively charged rod is brought near an isolated metal sphere on an insulating stand. CONDUCTION: touch the rod to the sphere. Electrons flow from the rod onto the sphere until both are at the same potential. Remove the rod: the sphere is left negative, the same sign as the rod, and the rod is now less negative than it was. INDUCTION: hold the rod close without touching. The sphere polarises - near side positive, far side negative - but its net charge is still zero. Now earth the far side with a wire: the repelled electrons escape to earth. Break the earth connection while the rod is still held in place. Only now remove the rod. The sphere is left with a net POSITIVE charge, opposite to the rod, and the rod's own charge is exactly what it was at the start. If instead you removed the rod before breaking the earth, electrons would flow straight back from earth and the sphere would end up neutral - which is the single most common way this is got wrong.

recapCandidates.topic: Why a function must be one-to-one before it can be inverted, and why the domain - not the formula - is what decides.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Inversion is learned as the three-step algorithm (write y = f(x), swap x and y, solve for y), and the algorithm runs happily on functions that have no inverse, so it produces an answer that looks right and nothing in the procedure flags the problem.
whyQuestions: What does f-inverse actually do to a number, in one sentence, without mentioning the algorithm?
If f sends both 2 and -2 to 4, what would f-inverse(4) have to be?
Why does that make the reversed pairing fail to be a function, rather than merely being awkward?
The formula x^2 has no inverse on R but does on [0, inf). The rule never changed, so what did?
Given that, what is wrong with saying 'the inverse of x^2 is sqrt(x)' without further qualification?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It defines the inverse as the reverse pairing - f-inverse takes an output of f back to the input that produced it - so that f-inverse(f(x)) = x, and not as a rearrangement recipe.
It shows that a many-to-one f makes that reversal ill-defined: the shared output would need two images, which violates the very 'exactly one output' clause that makes something a function in the first place.
It concludes that a function is a rule together with a domain, so restricting the domain to make f one-to-one is what creates the inverse, and that the horizontal line test is the graphical form of exactly this check.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Take f(x) = x^2 on domain R. Run the algorithm anyway: y = x^2, swap to get x = y^2, solve to get y = +/-sqrt(x). The '+/-' is the algorithm telling you it has failed - for x = 4 it offers both 2 and -2, so the result is not a function and f has no inverse. Check it against the definition: f(2) = 4 and f(-2) = 4, so f-inverse(4) would have to be 2 and -2 at once. Graphically, the horizontal line y = 4 meets the parabola twice. Now restrict the domain to [0, inf). The pairs (-2, 4), (-3, 9) and so on are gone, every horizontal line now meets the curve at most once, and the same algorithm returns y = +sqrt(x) only, a genuine function. Note what swapped: dom f = [0, inf) and ran f = [0, inf), so dom f-inverse = ran f = [0, inf). Restricting instead to (-inf, 0] is equally valid and gives f-inverse(x) = -sqrt(x) - which shows the inverse depends on the domain chosen, not on the formula x^2.
